1-1-1: A caring team, ready for a safety system behind it

Your team follows good hygiene and takes care with students who have allergies. Today, safety depends on individual effort: there are few records, no documented allergen controls, and changes happen only after a concern.
Start with the basics that protect everyone: food safety records and trained food handlers, allergen labels on every dish, and a short monthly review.
You can show your board and parents that food safety is managed, not left to chance.
A documented system lowers the risk of an incident, and an incident is the fastest way to lose the trust of families.
Parents, especially those of children with allergies, gain the peace of mind of knowing there is a system.
1-1-3: Regular reviews show intent; the safety basics come next
Reviewing menus and feedback from time to time shows a team that wants to improve. Day-to-day safety, though, still relies on good habits, and allergies are managed through staff memory.
Put records, food-handler training and regular inspections in place, and start labelling allergens on every menu.
Your reviews gain real substance when there are records to review.
Documented controls protect the institution if a question is ever raised by a parent or an inspector.
Families see safety handled the same way every day, not just on inspection days.
1-1-5: A data-led mindset, waiting for safety controls to measure
Using data to find gaps and test changes is a strength many institutions lack. The basics it should be measuring, documented safety checks and allergen controls, are not yet in place.
Apply your improvement approach to safety: set up records and inspections, an allergen register for every recipe, and track both in your reviews.
You already think in data; adding safety gives you a complete, measurable programme.
Measured safety is the strongest answer to any concern from families, inspectors or your board.
Parents see that safety gets the same attention as everything else.
